rationale: Bisort is a tiny (1697 text bytes, 14 functions), recursion-heavy Olden benchmark whose recursive cores (RandTree, Bimerge, bitonic sort) dominate both runtime and reverse-engineering value, so the table favors low-overhead structural passes: SUB gets the highest weights because instruction substitution adds strong per-function diversity at negligible runtime/size cost on such a small binary, and FLA is weighted nearly as high because control-flow flattening is the strongest defense for the deeply nested recursive/branchy code that constitutes almost all of this program. SPLIT is favored because the functions are small (largest is only 396 bytes), making basic-block splitting an effective and cheap way to obscure boundaries, while IBR gets moderate-high weights to break the predictable branch structure of the recursion and dispatch logic. BCF is kept at moderate benefit weights with suppressed cost weights since bogus control flow's code-size and runtime inflation is poorly absorbed by a 1.7 KB benchmark whose runtime is measured, and ICALL is weighted lowest because bisort contains almost no indirect-call sites to disguise (its calls are direct recursive/static calls), making its transformation mostly wasted overhead with added correctness exposure; IGV sits in between, providing modest protection for the few globals used by dealwithargs/args.c without significant cost. Overall the cost/risk dimension weights are held low across all passes so the feature-driven selector still applies passes where they help but avoids compounding runtime/size inflation on the hot recursive paths, preserving benchmark-representative timing and full correctness.
